title: Great Explorers · Episode 1
chapters: Ibn Battuta: the greatest traveller of the Middle Ages
Marco Polo and the Silk Road
Zheng He and the treasure fleets

units.t: Great Explorers. Episode one.
In this episode: Polynesian navigators, Ibn Battuta: the greatest traveller of the Middle Ages, Marco Polo and the Silk Road and Zheng He and the treasure fleets.
Part one. Polynesian navigators.
Without compasses or charts, Polynesian voyagers settled the vast Pacific, reading stars, swells and birds to find specks of land in an ocean.
The greatest migration.
The Polynesian triangle runs from Hawai'i in the north to Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west and Rapa Nui, Easter Island, in the south-east.
Each side is thousands of kilometres long, and most of the inside is open ocean dotted with tiny islands.
Finding them meant aiming for targets a few kilometres wide.
New Zealand was one of the last major places on Earth settled by humans, around 1250 to 1300 AD.
The story begins with the Lapita culture, named after a site in New Caledonia and known for its stamped pottery.
About 3,000 years ago, Lapita people reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture and languages took shape.
After a pause of over a thousand years, voyaging resumed about 1,000 years ago and spread people across the triangle.
Canoes built for settling.
Polynesians sailed large double-hulled canoes: two hulls joined by a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves.
The hulls were shaped with stone adzes and lashed together with coconut-fibre cord, with no metal at all.
The canoes were stable and fast, and could carry dozens of people along with taro, breadfruit, coconuts, pigs, dogs and chickens.
These weren't accidental drifts.
Genetic, linguistic and archaeological evidence shows deliberate, planned voyages of settlement.
Navigators often sailed into the prevailing winds, so the trip home would be downwind and a return stayed possible.
Reading the stars.
A master navigator memorised a 'star compass': the points on the horizon where many stars rise and set.
As one star climbed too high to be useful, the next along the same path took its place through the night.
Stars passing directly overhead revealed latitude, so a navigator could sail to the right latitude and then run along it to an island.
By day they used the Sun and the steady direction of the ocean swells.
This knowledge was passed down orally over many years of apprenticeship, often within families, and guarded carefully.
Reading the ocean.
Swells travel long distances in steady directions.
Skilled navigators felt them through the hull, even lying down, and noticed how islands bent and reflected them.
Seabirds such as terns and noddies fly out to sea to fish in the morning and back to land at dusk, pointing the way.
Because they range only a few dozen kilometres, they effectively widen each island into a much bigger target.
Clouds pile up over islands, a greenish tinge under them can reveal a lagoon, and floating plants and water colour offered more clues.
In 1769, the Ra'iatean priest and navigator Tupaia joined James Cook's Endeavour at Tahiti.
He guided the ship through nearby islands and helped draw a chart of more than 70, which scholars still debate how to read.
He also helped Cook speak with Māori, and died in Batavia in 1770.
Proof and revival.
For much of the twentieth century, some Western scholars doubted that Polynesians navigated deliberately, suggesting they drifted by accident.
In 1976, the double-hulled canoe Hōkūle'a, about 19 metres long, sailed some 4,000 kilometres from Hawai'i to Tahiti in roughly a month.
Its navigator was Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, using no instruments.
The voyage proved the methods worked and sparked a revival across the Pacific.
Piailug trained Hawaiian navigators such as Nainoa Thompson, breaking with tradition to share knowledge beyond his own people so it would survive.
Hōkūle'a sailed around the world from 2014 to 2017.
Polynesians probably reached South America too: the sweet potato grew across Polynesia before Europeans arrived, and a 2020 genetic study found contact with Native Americans around 1150 to 1230.
The key idea: Polynesian voyagers settled a vast triangle of Pacific islands, reaching some of the last places on Earth settled by humans.
Part two. Ibn Battuta: the greatest traveller of the Middle Ages.
In 1325 a young Moroccan set off on a pilgrimage to Mecca.
He came home almost a quarter of a century later, having seen more of the world than anyone of his age.
Leaving Tangier.
In June 1325, 21-year-old Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, in what is now Morocco, to make the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims aim to complete at least once.
He came from a family of legal scholars and was trained in Islamic law.
He set out alone, and later described weeping at leaving his parents.
He expected the journey to take a year or two.
Instead he would not return for around 24 years.
His travels took him across North Africa, the Middle East, East Africa, Central Asia, India, South-East Asia and, by his account, China, a distance often estimated at well over 100,000 kilometres.
A world connected.
How could a young man travel so far in the 1300s?
Much of the answer lies in his world.
Islam had spread from Spain and West Africa to India and parts of South-East Asia.
Across it, educated Muslims shared Arabic as a language of learning, followed the same broad body of Islamic law and recognised each other's scholarship.
A trained legal scholar like Ibn Battuta could arrive in a distant city and be welcomed by rulers and religious leaders, who often gave travellers gifts, lodging and sometimes jobs.
Pilgrim caravans, trade routes and religious lodges supported him along the way.
It was a network as much as a map.
Mecca, Africa and Delhi.
Ibn Battuta reached Mecca in 1326 but kept exploring, travelling through Iraq and Persia.
Around 1330 he sailed down the Red Sea and East African coast, visiting trading cities such as Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa, which traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean.
He later crossed Anatolia and the steppes of Central Asia, joining a Mongol khan's court.
Next he sought India, where the Sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, was famous for generosity to foreign scholars.
In the 1330s he was appointed a qadi, or judge, on a large salary, and stayed about eight years.
But the Sultan was also notorious for sudden cruelty, and Ibn Battuta feared for his life at one point.
Chosen to lead an embassy to China, he saw his party attacked and the gift ships wrecked.
Islands and China.
Having lost the embassy, and afraid to return to Delhi, Ibn Battuta went to the Maldives.
He served as a judge there for around a year, married several times and tried, with mixed success, to impose stricter religious law.
He visited Sri Lanka, climbing the sacred mountain Adam's Peak, then continued to Bengal and South-East Asia.
By his account he reached China in the 1340s, describing its ports, paper money and porcelain.
Some historians doubt how far into China he really went, because parts of this section are vague or seem borrowed from other sources.
Even so, his descriptions show a world joined by busy sea trade.
Mali and the Rihla.
Ibn Battuta returned to Morocco in 1349 and learned that his mother had died of the plague.
Soon he was travelling again: to Granada, then in the early 1350s across the Sahara by camel caravan to the Mali Empire, famous for its gold.
He visited the ruler, Mansa Sulayman, and Timbuktu.
He admired the safe travel, but disliked some customs, revealing his biases.
The Sultan of Fez asked him to record his journeys.
He dictated to a scholar, Ibn Juzayy, and the book, the Rihla, journey, was completed around 1355.
Historians read it carefully: it was written from memory years later, some passages seem copied from earlier writers, and a few journeys may be exaggerated.
Yet it is one of the richest records of the fourteenth century, and a lunar crater bears his name.
The key idea: A 21-year-old set out for Mecca in 1325 and did not come home for around 24 years.
Part three. Marco Polo and the Silk Road.
A young Venetian travelled to the court of Kublai Khan and wrote the book that made Europe dream of the East.
A web, not a road.
The Silk Road wasn't one road but a web of land and sea routes across Central Asia, the Middle East and India, active from around the 100s BC.
The name is modern, coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.
Silk, spices, porcelain, horses, glass and paper travelled along it, usually through many traders' hands, so few people ever travelled its whole length.
Ideas moved too: Buddhism spread from India to China, and papermaking moved west.
So did disease, including, eventually, the Black Death in the 1300s.
The Mongol peace.
In the 1200s, Genghis Khan and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.
The conquests were brutal, and resisting cities were often destroyed.
But once established, the Mongols protected trade routes and travellers, ran relay stations for messengers and tolerated many religions, a period sometimes called the Pax Mongolica.
This allowed European merchants and missionaries to travel all the way to China, now ruled by Genghis's grandson, Kublai Khan.
Venice to Kublai's court.
Niccolò and Maffeo Polo, Venetian merchants, had visited Kublai Khan in the 1260s.
In 1271 they set out again, taking Niccolò's 17-year-old son Marco.
The journey through Persia, Central Asia and the Gobi Desert took about three and a half years.
Venice was a wealthy trading republic, and its merchants were used to long journeys, though few went as far as the Polos.
According to Marco, Kublai took a liking to him and sent him on missions across China.
He described paper money accepted across the empire, black stones burned for heat, coal, a postal relay of thousands of horses, and cities like Hangzhou that dwarfed Venice.
Kublai ruled from Khanbaliq, on the site of Beijing, with a summer palace at Shangdu, the 'Xanadu' of later poetry.
Some claims about his own importance were probably exaggerated.
Home and the book.
After about 17 years in China, the Polos wanted to go home, but Kublai was reluctant.
Their chance came when the Mongol princess Kököchin needed an escort to Persia to marry its ruler.
They sailed from southern China around 1291, via Sumatra, Sri Lanka and India.
The voyage took about two years and many died.
Her intended husband had died, so she married his son.
The Polos reached Venice in 1295.
Marco was captured in a war with Genoa, probably around 1298.
In prison he told his stories to Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of romances, who wrote them in French.
Hand-copied in many versions, the book has no single original.
In Italy it became 'Il Milione', perhaps for his 'million' tall tales.
Marco died in Venice in 1324.
Truth and legacy.
Sceptics note that the book omits the Great Wall, tea and foot binding, and that Chinese records don't name him.

Supporters reply that the Great Wall people picture was built later, under the Ming; that he mixed mainly with Mongols; and that he gave accurate details, such as salt production, paper money and the princess's voyage, which a Persian source also records.
Most historians accept that he went, even if some stories were embellished.
The Travels shaped European images of Asia for centuries, and the 1375 Catalan Atlas drew on it.
Columbus owned a heavily annotated printed copy, which survives in Seville.
When the Mongol Empire fragmented and the Ottomans rose, overland trade became harder, pushing Europeans towards sea routes and the Age of Discovery.
Venice's airport bears his name.
The key idea: The Silk Road was a web of land and sea routes that carried goods, ideas and diseases between China and the Mediterranean.
Part four. Zheng He and the treasure fleets.
Decades before Columbus, a Chinese admiral led some of the largest fleets the world had ever seen across the Indian Ocean.
Then China stopped sending them.
From captive to admiral.
Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, southwest China, into a Muslim family named Ma.
His father and grandfather had reportedly made the pilgrimage to Mecca.
When Ming armies conquered Yunnan, the boy was captured, castrated, as was common for captive boys entering royal service, and sent to serve the prince Zhu Di.
He grew into a tall, capable soldier and adviser and helped Zhu Di win a bloody civil war and seize the throne in 1402.
Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor, one of the most ambitious rulers in Chinese history.
He rewarded his loyal eunuch with the surname Zheng, and later gave him command of an enterprise on a scale the world had rarely seen.
Seven great voyages.
The first voyage set out in 1405.
Chinese records describe over 300 ships carrying around 27,000 people: sailors, soldiers, interpreters, doctors, craftsmen and officials.
Across seven voyages, ending in 1433, the fleets visited Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka, then India's Calicut and Hormuz at the entrance to the Persian Gulf.
Later voyages reached Arabia and East Africa, including Mogadishu and Malindi, and some crew visited Mecca.
They sailed with the seasonal monsoon winds.
The largest "treasure ships" are described in a later Ming source as roughly 120 to 140 metres long.
Some historians accept this; many doubt wooden hulls could be so long, and suggest 60 to 75 metres, still enormous.
Nobody disputes the fleets were vast and well organised.
Prestige, not conquest.
The fleets did not set out to found colonies.

Their main purpose was to show the new emperor's might and wealth, gather tribute, and bring foreign rulers into a system in which they acknowledged his supremacy and received gifts and trade in return.
But the voyages were not entirely peaceful.
Soldiers fought a pirate leader near Palembang in Sumatra, and in Sri Lanka a local king was captured and taken to China.
One charming result was a giraffe.
In 1414 envoys from Bengal brought one to China, originally from Malindi.
Courtiers declared it a qilin, a gentle creature of legend whose appearance signalled a wise and virtuous ruler.
For an emperor who had taken power violently, heaven's approval walking into the palace on four long legs had obvious political value.
Why the voyages stopped.
Zheng He probably died around 1433, during or soon after the seventh voyage, and he may have been buried at sea.
No fleet on that scale ever sailed again.
Historians point to several reasons.
The voyages were extremely expensive, and the court faced costly pressures on land, especially from Mongol forces on the northern frontier and the building of the new capital at Beijing.
Confucian officials were often hostile to the powerful palace eunuchs who ran the voyages, and saw them as a wasteful vanity.
Later Ming governments also restricted private overseas trade for long periods.
A story says officials deliberately destroyed the voyage records, though how much was lost and why is still debated.
Myth and memory.
Zheng He's story has attracted wild claims.
A popular book published in 2002 argued that his fleets discovered America and sailed around the world in 1421.
Historians have firmly rejected this: there is no credible evidence for it in Chinese or other records, or in archaeology.
The real story needs no exaggeration.
Around Southeast Asia, temples and shrines remember him, including in Malacca, Semarang and Surabaya, and he is respected by both Chinese and Muslim communities.
In modern China he is a symbol of peaceful maritime exchange.
Decades before Portuguese ships reached India, Chinese fleets had crossed the same ocean, and then chose not to come back.
The key idea: Zheng He, a Muslim captive from Yunnan, rose through the household of Prince Zhu Di to command the Ming treasure fleets.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What made settling the Polynesian triangle such a feat?
Answer. Tiny islands lay far apart across open ocean.
Question two. Why did Ibn Battuta leave Tangier in 1325?
Answer. To make the pilgrimage to Mecca.
Question three. What was the Silk Road?
Answer. A network of trade routes from China westward.
Question four. How did Zheng He, once a captive, rise to command the fleets?
Answer. Through loyal service to a future emperor.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
